title: Leftovers
summary: The shop's config file is locked down tight. But developers have a habit of leaving copies behind…
briefing:
Chapter 2 begins. DotTech has opened a web shop on the server dottech-shop, and you have **written permission** to test it.

The shop's database password is in `/var/www/shop/config.php`, and that file is properly locked: only root may read it. Good!

But Sam, the developer, edits files directly on the live server. Text editors and nervous developers love to leave copies behind – files ending in `.bak`, `.old`, `.orig` or `~`. A copy doesn't get the original's permissions.

Find a leftover copy of the config and read the database password.
objective: Find a leftover copy of the shop's config and read the database password. It is the flag.
debrief:
Found it! The real `config.php` was locked, but `config.php.bak` – a copy Sam made "just in case" – could be read by anyone.

You used `ls -la` to spot the copies and `find` with a pattern like `*.bak` to search for them everywhere. Attackers do exactly this: on web servers they even try to download `config.php.bak` straight from the browser, because the server won't run it as code and simply sends the text – passwords and all.

The lessons for DotTech: never edit files on a live server, keep secrets out of the web folder, and clean up backup copies. Better still, don't keep passwords in files at all.
hints: The locked file has a copy somewhere, and copies usually get a new ending like `.bak` or `.old`. Look closely at everything in the shop's folder – including the details of each file.
`ls -la /var/www/shop` shows every file with its permissions. To search the whole computer, use `find / -name "*.bak" 2>/dev/null` (the `2>/dev/null` hides the 'Permission denied' messages).
